title: How do Tibetans avoid altitude sickness?
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss how Tibetans live at very high altitude without suffering hypoxia and altitude sickness. They explain hypoxia and its symptoms, describe a Case Western study finding that Tibetans keep more nitric oxide in their bodies, which dilates blood vessels and eases oxygen delivery. They contrast this with Francois Viault's 1890 finding that Andean highlanders have higher red blood cell counts, and note that Ethiopian highlanders show no known adaptation. They speculate about how highlanders handle a return to sea level. The episode closes with a sponsor read and a plug for a HowStuffWorks article on home devaluation.

segments.title: Opening sponsor reads and banter
segments.summary: Opens with a sponsor read for the Go to Meeting online meeting service and a camera ad, followed by Josh and Chuck's banter about travel and Tibet.

segments.title: Life on the roof of the world
segments.summary: Josh describes Tibetan mountain villages at about 16,000 feet, compares them to Denver, and explains altitude sickness symptoms such as nausea, dizziness, vomiting and shortness of breath. He notes that Tibetans seem unaffected.

segments.title: Hypoxia in Tibetans and the Case Western study
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh explain hypoxia as a lack of oxygen in the blood. Researchers found Tibetans are hypoxic but show no symptoms. A Case Western team measured exhaled air and found Tibetans keep more nitric oxide, which dilates blood vessels and makes oxygen delivery easier.

segments.title: Convergent versus separate high-altitude adaptations
segments.summary: The hosts discuss evolution and isolation, asking whether all high-altitude groups adapt the same way. They describe Francois Viault's 1890 visit to the Andes, where he found higher red blood cell counts, and hemoglobin's role in carrying oxygen.

segments.title: Ethiopian highlanders and open questions
segments.summary: Josh introduces the Ethiopian highlands, where residents show no known adaptation such as extra red blood cells or altered oxygen levels. The hosts say the mechanism may not have been found yet and that they should be symptomatic.

segments.title: Returning to sea level and Amsterdam
segments.summary: Chuck wonders how Tibetan and Ethiopian highlanders cope when they go down to sea level, such as a weekend in Amsterdam. Josh suggests they might feel high. The hosts summarize what is known.

segments.title: Closing plug for home devaluation article
segments.summary: A HowStuffWorks plug for Jessica Toothman's article 'Top five things that devalue your house', with a closing reminder to visit the website and send feedback, plus a repeat of the camera ad.
